metric_rationale: The experimental trials are specifically designed so that Tallying and WADD consistently predict opposite choices. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic's predictions (i.e., choosing the option that wins on the majority of features, regardless of magnitude), we can perfectly discriminate between the two models. Data simulated under Tallying will yield a metric value close to 1.0 (modulo lapse rate), whereas data simulated under WADD will yield a value closer to 0.0, resulting in a massive and highly significant gap.

This metric isolates trials 1 and 5, where the predictions of Tallying and WADD are diametrically opposed and highly robust to parameter variations. In these trials, option A wins on a majority of features (features 2 and 3) but by small margins, leading Tallying to deterministically prefer A. Conversely, option B wins on the single most valid feature (feature 1) by a massive margin, which overwhelms the small deficits on the other features in a compensatory model, leading WADD to strongly prefer B. The metric calculates the proportion of choices for option B across these specific trials. It will yield a value near 0 for Tallying and near 1 for WADD.

By design, the chosen experimental trials perfectly dissociate Take The Best (TTB) and Weighted Additive (WADD) models: on every single trial, the two models predict opposite choices. This metric directly computes the proportion of choices that are consistent with the lexicographic TTB rule. For data generated by TTB, this metric will be close to 1.0 (subject to lapse noise). For data generated by WADD, it will be close to 0.0, as WADD reliably chooses the compensatory option. This ensures a massive mean separation with very tight per-subject variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject makes the choice predicted by the non-compensatory Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. The experimental design specifically pits TTB against the compensatory Weighted Additive (WADD) rule on 7 out of 8 trial types, meaning TTB will consistently score very high on this metric (close to 1.0, minus lapse rate) while WADD will score very low, providing strong discriminability.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with the strictly greater unweighted sum of features. Under the Random Guessing theory, subjects choose options randomly, so this metric will tightly cluster around 0.5. Under the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, the chosen experimental design ensures that the option with the higher unweighted sum also heavily dominates in the weighted sum (e.g., [10, 10, 10] vs [0, 0, 0]). Because the provided WADD policy deterministically selects the option with the highest probability (via argmax), WADD subjects will consistently choose the dominating option, yielding a metric value close to 1.0.

WADD predicts that the probability of choosing option A will vary systematically across different trial types depending on the validity-weighted differences in feature values (ranging from near 0 to near 1). In contrast, Random Guessing predicts a flat 50% choice rate for option A across all trial types. By calculating the variance of the choice rate of option A across the unique trial types, we can clearly distinguish the two models: WADD will produce a high variance, while Random Guessing will produce a variance close to zero (driven only by binomial noise).

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chose the option that dominates on a strict majority of features. Under Random Guessing, this proportion will be exactly 0.5 (since they ignore features). Under the Single Random Feature heuristic, subjects are far more likely to choose the option with more feature wins (e.g., 100% on 4-0 trials, 75% on 3-1 trials), leading to a score substantially higher than 0.5.

This metric calculates the covariance between the subject's choice and the theoretical advantage of Option A under the Single Random Feature (SRF) theory. For the Random Guessing theory, choices are independent of the options' features, yielding an expected value of 0. For the SRF theory, subjects are more likely to choose Option A when it wins on more features, yielding a strictly positive expected value. The vectorized implementation ensures robust and fast execution.
